notes:
Stress and strain

  • Stress $= F/A$ (unit: pascal, Pa = N m$^{-2}$). The three types are longitudinal, shearing (tangential) and volume (hydraulic) stress.
  • Strain = (change in dimension)/(original dimension) — dimensionless. Longitudinal strain $= \Delta L/L$; shear strain = angle of shear; volumetric strain $= \Delta V/V$.
  • Hooke's law: within the proportional (elastic) limit, stress $\propto$ strain.

Elastic moduli

ModulusDefined byApplicable to
Young's, $Y$$\dfrac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \dfrac{FL}{A\Delta L}$solids only
Shear (rigidity), $G$$\dfrac{\text{shear stress}}{\text{shear strain}}$solids only
Bulk, $K$$-V\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V}$solids, liquids and gases
  • Compressibility $= 1/K$.
  • Poisson's ratio $\sigma = \dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}$; for most materials $\sigma \approx 0.2$–$0.4$ (theoretical range $-1$ to $0.5$).

Stress–strain curve

  • Proportional limit: stress $\propto$ strain (Hooke's law valid).
  • Elastic limit: the maximum stress after which removing the load still restores the original shape; beyond it, deformation becomes permanent (plastic).
  • Yield point, then ultimate tensile strength (the maximum stress the material can bear), and finally the fracture (breaking) point.

Elastic potential energy

  • Energy stored per unit volume of a stretched wire $= \frac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain} = \frac12Y(\text{strain})^2$.
  • Work done in stretching a wire obeying Hooke's law by $\Delta L$ under a final force $F$: $W = \frac12F\Delta L$.

Key results

  • Elongation $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$: for the same load and material, $\Delta L \propto L$ and $\Delta L \propto 1/A$ (i.e. $\propto 1/r^2$ for a wire of radius $r$).
  • Strain produced by a given stress depends only on the material's Young's modulus, not on the length or cross-section of the sample.

Exam tip

KCET usually sets about 1 question from this chapter, most often a direct Young's-modulus or elongation numerical, occasionally a stress–strain-curve or moduli-comparison concept question.

questions.q: The SI unit of stress is
questions.explanation: Stress $= F/A$, so its unit is N m$^{-2}$, which is the pascal (Pa).
questions.trick: Stress $=F/A$, unit N m$^{-2}$ $=$ pascal directly.

questions.q: Strain, defined as the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension, has
questions.explanation: Strain is a ratio of two like quantities (e.g. $\Delta L/L$), so all units cancel and it is dimensionless.
questions.trick: Ratio of two like quantities cancels units $\Rightarrow$ strain is dimensionless.

questions.q: A wire of length 1 m and cross-sectional area 1 mm$^2$ stretches by 0.5 mm under a load of 100 N. Its Young's modulus is
questions.explanation: $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\Delta L} = \dfrac{100\times1}{(1\times10^{-6})(5\times10^{-4})} = \dfrac{100}{5\times10^{-10}} = 2\times10^{11}$ Pa.
questions.trick: $Y=FL/(A\Delta L)$: plug values, watch mm$^2\to$m$^2$ and mm$\to$m conversions.

questions.q: A wire of length 2 m, cross-sectional area $1\times10^{-6}$ m$^2$ and Young's modulus $2\times10^{11}$ Pa is stretched by a force of 100 N. Its elongation is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} = \dfrac{100\times2}{(1\times10^{-6})(2\times10^{11})} = \dfrac{200}{2\times10^{5}} = 1\times10^{-3}$ m = 1 mm.
questions.trick: $\Delta L=FL/(AY)$ — direct substitution, no need to find $Y$ separately.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and cross-sectional area, but of lengths $L$ and $2L$, are stretched by the same load. The ratio of their elongations (shorter : longer) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = FL/(AY) \propto L$ for fixed $F, A, Y$, so the elongations are in the ratio $L:2L = 1:2$.
questions.trick: $\Delta L\propto L$ for same $F,A,Y$ — ratio equals length ratio.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and length, but of radii $r$ and $2r$, are stretched by the same load. The ratio of their elongations (thinner : thicker) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L \propto 1/A \propto 1/r^2$. Ratio $= (2r)^2 : r^2 = 4:1$ for thinner to thicker.
questions.trick: $\Delta L\propto1/r^2$ — thinner wire stretches more, ratio $=(r_2/r_1)^2$.

questions.q: A material under a stress of $1\times10^8$ Pa develops a strain of $1\times10^{-3}$. The elastic potential energy stored per unit volume is
questions.explanation: Energy density $= \frac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain} = \frac12\times10^8\times10^{-3} = 5\times10^4$ J m$^{-3}$.
questions.trick: Energy density $=\frac12\times$stress$\times$strain — half, don't forget the $\frac12$.

questions.q: The reciprocal of the bulk modulus of a substance is called its
questions.explanation: Compressibility is defined as $1/K$, where $K$ is the bulk modulus.
questions.trick: Compressibility $=1/K$; recall it as bulk modulus's reciprocal.

questions.q: For most engineering materials, Poisson's ratio typically lies between
questions.explanation: Experimentally, Poisson's ratio for common metals and alloys is usually in the range 0.2 to 0.4 (theoretical limits are $-1$ to $0.5$).
questions.trick: Memorise: real materials' $\sigma\approx0.2$–$0.4$, theoretical cap 0.5.

questions.q: In a stress–strain curve, the point up to which stress is directly proportional to strain is called the
questions.explanation: Hooke's law (stress $\propto$ strain) holds only up to the proportional limit; beyond it the curve is no longer linear.
questions.trick: Proportional limit = where stress-strain graph is still a straight line.

questions.q: For the same applied stress, steel shows much smaller strain than rubber. This means, in terms of Young's modulus,
options: steel is more elastic than rubber (steel has a higher Young's modulus)
Young's modulus cannot be compared between them
steel and rubber are equally elastic
steel is less elastic than rubber
questions.explanation: Elasticity is measured by how strongly a material resists deformation; smaller strain for the same stress means a higher $Y = \text{stress/strain}$, i.e. steel is more elastic.
questions.trick: Less strain for same stress $\Rightarrow$ higher $Y=$stress/strain $\Rightarrow$ more elastic.

questions.q: The shear (rigidity) modulus relates tangential stress to shear strain and can be meaningfully defined for
options: none of the states of matter
solids only, since a shape-restoring force is required
questions.explanation: Only solids can sustain a shearing (tangential) stress without continuously deforming; liquids and gases flow instead, so shear modulus is not defined for them.
questions.trick: Shear needs a fixed shape to resist sliding $\Rightarrow$ solids only.

questions.q: Bulk modulus can be meaningfully defined and measured for
questions.explanation: Volume (hydraulic) stress can be applied to any state of matter, so bulk modulus is defined for solids, liquids and gases.
questions.trick: Bulk modulus works wherever volume can be squeezed: solids, liquids, gases.

questions.q: If a wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit and the load is then removed, the wire
options: shows zero strain at all times
returns exactly to its original length
does not return to its original length; a permanent (plastic) deformation remains
questions.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit the material behaves plastically, so some permanent deformation remains even after the load is removed.
questions.trick: Past elastic limit $\Rightarrow$ permanent (plastic) set remains on unloading.

questions.q: A wire obeying Hooke's law stretches by 2 mm under a final applied force of 200 N (force increases linearly from zero). The work done in stretching it is
questions.explanation: $W = \frac12F\Delta L = \frac12\times200\times0.002 = 0.2$ J.
questions.trick: Linear force build-up $\Rightarrow$ $W=\frac12F\Delta L$ (area of force-extension triangle).

questions.q: Young's modulus and shear (rigidity) modulus are elastic properties defined only for
questions.explanation: Only solids can sustain the tensile and shearing stresses used to define Young's modulus and shear modulus.
questions.trick: Tensile and shear stresses need rigidity $\Rightarrow$ $Y,G$ defined for solids only.

questions.q: Two rods of the same material but different lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$ are subjected to the same tensile stress. The ratio of the strains produced in them is
questions.explanation: Strain $= \text{stress}/Y$ depends only on the material's Young's modulus and the applied stress, not on the length of the rod, so both rods have equal strain.
questions.trick: Strain $=$ stress$/Y$ — no length or area dependence at all.

questions.q: The maximum stress a material can withstand and still return exactly to its original dimensions once the load is removed defines its
questions.explanation: This is precisely the definition of the elastic limit; stresses beyond it cause permanent (plastic) deformation.
questions.trick: "Returns exactly, still recoverable" is the textbook definition of elastic limit.

questions.q: Young's modulus of most metals
options: becomes infinite at very high temperature
questions.explanation: Increasing temperature generally weakens interatomic bonding forces, reducing the material's stiffness, so Young's modulus decreases with rising temperature for most metals.
questions.trick: Heat weakens interatomic bonds $\Rightarrow$ $Y$ falls as temperature rises.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material, having different lengths $L_1,L_2$ and the same cross-sectional area, are joined end to end and stretched by a common load $F$. The total elongation of the combination is
questions.explanation: In series, both wires carry the same load $F$; total elongation = sum of individual elongations = $\dfrac{FL_1}{AY}+\dfrac{FL_2}{AY}=\dfrac{F(L_1+L_2)}{AY}$.
questions.trick: Series wires: same $F$ in each, elongations add $\Rightarrow \Delta L\propto(L_1+L_2)$.

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and length but cross-sectional areas $A_1$ and $A_2$ are fixed side by side between two rigid supports and jointly support a load $F$. Since both stretch by the same amount, the load shared by each wire is proportional to
options: the inverse of its cross-sectional area
questions.explanation: With $\Delta L = FL/(AY)$ and equal $L,Y,\Delta L$ for both wires, $F\propto A$; the wire with the larger area bears proportionally more load.
questions.trick: Parallel wires: equal $\Delta L$ forces $F\propto A$ (same $L,Y$).

questions.q: Using $Y=3K(1-2\sigma)$, if a material has bulk modulus $K=1.6\times10^{11}$ Pa and Poisson's ratio $\sigma=0.25$, its Young's modulus is
questions.trick: Recall $Y=3K(1-2\sigma)$ — a direct plug-in relation between moduli.

questions.q: Using $Y=2G(1+\sigma)$, for a material with $Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa and Poisson's ratio $\sigma=0.25$, the rigidity (shear) modulus $G$ is
questions.explanation: $G=\dfrac{Y}{2(1+\sigma)}=\dfrac{2\times10^{11}}{2\times1.25}=8\times10^{10}$ Pa.
questions.trick: Recall $G=Y/[2(1+\sigma)]$ — the other modulus-linking formula.

questions.q: A material subjected to repeated loading and unloading cycles, each time staying within its elastic limit, gradually loses some of its elastic strength over time. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: Repeated stress cycling weakens a material's elastic response over time even though each load stays within the elastic limit — this is elastic fatigue, important in the design of bridges and machine parts under cyclic loads.
questions.trick: Repeated elastic-limit cycling weakening the material = elastic fatigue, not creep.

questions.q: The breaking stress (tensile strength) of a given material for wires of different lengths and cross-sections is
options: inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area
proportional to the length of the wire
a constant, independent of the wire's length or area
questions.explanation: Breaking stress is an intrinsic property of the material and does not depend on the sample's dimensions; only the breaking force ($=$ breaking stress $\times$ area) depends on the cross-sectional area.
questions.trick: Breaking stress is a material constant; only breaking force scales with area.

questions.q: A wire of volume $2\times10^{-6}$ m$^3$ is under a stress of $1\times10^8$ Pa producing a strain of $1\times10^{-3}$. The total elastic potential energy stored in the wire is
questions.explanation: Energy density $=\frac12\times\text{stress}\times\text{strain}=\frac12\times10^8\times10^{-3}=5\times10^4$ J m$^{-3}$; total energy $=5\times10^4\times2\times10^{-6}=0.1$ J.
questions.trick: Total PE $=$ energy density $\times$ volume — multiply the $\frac12$stress$\cdot$strain result.

questions.q: A ductile material such as copper, compared to a brittle material such as glass, typically shows
options: a long plastic region with significant elongation between the yield point and fracture
fracture almost immediately after the elastic limit is crossed, with negligible plastic deformation
questions.explanation: Ductile materials undergo considerable plastic deformation (elongation, necking) before breaking, unlike brittle materials, which fracture soon after the elastic limit with little plastic flow.
questions.trick: Ductile = long plastic stretch before break; brittle snaps soon after yield.

questions.q: Rubber-like materials (elastomers) show large strains for comparatively small stresses, and their loading and unloading stress-strain curves do not coincide (elastic hysteresis). This property makes rubber well suited for
options: replacing steel in load-bearing structural beams
precision measuring instruments requiring exact linear response
shock absorbers and vibration dampers, since the enclosed loop area represents energy dissipated as heat
questions.explanation: The hysteresis loop's area equals the energy dissipated per cycle as heat, which is exactly the damping behaviour desired in shock absorbers and vibration mounts.
questions.trick: Hysteresis loop area $=$ heat dissipated per cycle $\Rightarrow$ ideal for dampers.

questions.q: A steel rod is rigidly clamped at both ends so its length cannot change, and its temperature is then raised by 50°C. Taking $Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa and $\alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ for steel, the thermal stress developed in the rod is
questions.explanation: Since the length is fixed, the strain that would otherwise occur is entirely converted to stress: thermal stress $=Y\alpha\Delta T = 2\times10^{11}\times1.2\times10^{-5}\times50 = 1.2\times10^8$ Pa.
questions.trick: Clamped ends: thermal stress $=Y\alpha\Delta T$, strain fully converts to stress.

questions.q: Arrange steel, copper and rubber in decreasing order of Young's modulus.
questions.explanation: Steel is stiffer (Y $\approx 2\times10^{11}$ Pa) than copper ($\approx1.1\times10^{11}$ Pa), and both are far stiffer than rubber (Y of order $10^6$ Pa).
questions.trick: Stiffness order: steel $\gg$ copper $\gg$ rubber (rubber's $Y\sim10^6$ Pa).

questions.q: A solid sphere of bulk modulus $2\times10^{10}$ Pa is subjected to a uniform pressure increase of $2\times10^6$ Pa. The fractional decrease in its volume is
questions.explanation: Volumetric strain $=\Delta P/K = (2\times10^6)/(2\times10^{10}) = 1\times10^{-4}$.
questions.trick: Volumetric strain $=\Delta P/K$ — direct substitution gives fractional decrease.

questions.q: A steel wire of length 2.5 m and cross-sectional area $0.5\times10^{-6}$ m$^2$ ($Y=2\times10^{11}$ Pa) has an 8 kg mass hung from it. Taking $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, the elongation produced is
questions.explanation: $F=mg=80$ N. $\Delta L=\dfrac{FL}{AY}=\dfrac{80\times2.5}{0.5\times10^{-6}\times2\times10^{11}}=\dfrac{200}{1\times10^{5}}=2\times10^{-3}$ m $=2$ mm.
questions.trick: $\Delta L=FL/(AY)$ with $F=mg$ — convert mm$^2$ area to m$^2$ first.

questions.q: Two wires of the same length and cross-sectional area, but made of materials with Young's moduli $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ ($Y_1=2Y_2$), are stretched by the same load. The ratio of their elongations $\Delta L_1:\Delta L_2$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L \propto 1/Y$ for fixed $F,L,A$; since $Y_1=2Y_2$, $\Delta L_1:\Delta L_2 = Y_2:Y_1 = 1:2$.
questions.trick: $\Delta L\propto1/Y$ for same $F,L,A$ — stiffer material stretches less.

questions.q: Within the elastic limit, the potential energy stored in a stretched wire arises from
options: the gravitational potential energy of the wire
heat generated due to friction between atoms
the kinetic energy of vibrating atoms
work done against the internal restoring (interatomic) forces as atoms are displaced from their equilibrium positions
questions.explanation: Stretching a wire displaces its atoms from their equilibrium separations; the work done against the interatomic restoring forces is stored as elastic potential energy, recoverable when the load is removed.
questions.trick: Elastic PE = work done against interatomic restoring forces on stretching.

questions.q: When the pressure on a liquid is increased by $4\times10^6$ Pa, its volume decreases by 0.02%. The bulk modulus of the liquid is
questions.explanation: $K=\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta V/V}=\dfrac{4\times10^6}{2\times10^{-4}}=2\times10^{10}$ Pa.
questions.trick: $K=\Delta P/(\Delta V/V)$ — convert the percentage to a fraction first.

questions.q: On a stress-strain graph, between the proportional limit and the elastic limit, a material
options: still returns exactly to its original dimensions on removing the load, even though stress is no longer strictly proportional to strain
questions.explanation: Up to the elastic limit (which lies slightly beyond the proportional limit for many materials), the deformation is fully recoverable even though the stress-strain relation is no longer linear in this small intermediate region.
questions.trick: Between proportional and elastic limits: nonlinear but still fully recoverable.

questions.q: Wires A and B of the same material have radii in the ratio 2:1 and lengths in the ratio 1:2. The same load is applied to both. The ratio of their elongations $\Delta L_A:\Delta L_B$ is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L \propto L/r^2$. $\dfrac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B}=\dfrac{L_A/r_A^2}{L_B/r_B^2}=\dfrac{1/4}{2}=\dfrac18$, i.e. $1:8$.
questions.trick: $\Delta L\propto L/r^2$ — combine both ratios, radius squared dominates.

questions.q: For an ideal liquid at rest, which of the following is true?
options: Young's modulus is nonzero but shear modulus is zero
The shear (rigidity) modulus is zero, while the bulk modulus has a finite, nonzero value
Both Young's modulus and shear modulus are well defined and nonzero
questions.explanation: A liquid cannot sustain a static shearing stress (it flows), so its shear modulus is zero, but it strongly resists a uniform change in volume, so its bulk modulus is finite and generally large.
questions.trick: Liquids: zero shear modulus (flows), but finite, large bulk modulus.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: Bulk modulus is defined only for solids.
Poisson's ratio can exceed 1 for common engineering materials.
The strain produced in a stretched wire depends only on the applied stress and the material's Young's modulus, not on the wire's length or cross-section.
Shear (rigidity) modulus can be defined for liquids at rest.
questions.explanation: Strain $=\text{stress}/Y$ is fixed once the stress and material are fixed, independent of the sample's length or area. The other statements are false: Poisson's ratio for real materials is theoretically capped at 0.5, bulk modulus applies to solids, liquids and gases, and liquids at rest cannot sustain shear stress.
questions.trick: Eliminate the wrong absolutes; strain depending only on stress/$Y$ is the true one.

questions.q: On the stress-strain graph of a ductile metal, the region just after the yield point, where the material continues to elongate substantially even though the stress increases only slightly, is called
questions.explanation: Beyond the yield point, the material deforms plastically with large increases in strain for only small increases in stress, until it reaches the ultimate tensile strength and eventually fractures.
questions.trick: Big strain jump for tiny stress rise right after yield = plastic region.
